KnowLM Workshop @ ACL 2025Internal knowledge and context

Understanding the Interplay between Parametric and Contextual Knowledge for Large Language Models

Sitao Cheng1, Liangming Pan2, Xunjian Yin1, Xinyi Wang1, William Yang Wang1

1 University of California, Santa Barbara · 2 University of Arizona

Paper ↗Code ↗Data ↗

Providing relevant context can make a model less willing to use facts it already knows; EchoQA tests when internal knowledge and external information work together or interfere.

Result
Llama 3.1-70B answers Unknown 62.72% of the time with complementary context, vs 23.89% with no context and 0.08% with all facts supplied.
New vs prior
Knowledge-conflict studies (Xie et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024) test one relationship at a time; EchoQA compares four kinds of context in one benchmark.
Limitation
The instructions that restore parametric knowledge must tell the model its context is insufficient, which the authors call impractical.
01 / The research question

Knowing both facts is not the same as combining them

Retrieval often supplies only the missing part of an answer, and the model must connect it with parametric knowledge, the facts stored in its weights. This differs from deciding whether to trust a passage that contradicts memory: both sources are correct, but neither suffices alone. EchoQA tests this complementary case alongside supportive, conflicting, and irrelevant context.

A correct answer does not prove composition either: without context, a model can infer an artificial entity's properties from its name and then eliminate answer options.

Closest prior work

Earlier studies examine one relationship at a time: context that conflicts with what the model knows (Wang et al., 2023b; Xie et al., 2024) or irrelevant context (Wu et al., 2024). ConflictQA (Xie et al., 2024) places the model's own elicited evidence and conflicting evidence together in the prompt and asks it to choose; EchoQA puts only the contextual knowledge in the prompt, so the model must draw on its parametric knowledge unprompted. It also adds the complementary case, built from new entity profiles rather than the entity-description substitutions of earlier multi-hop datasets, so that the context is new to the model.

02 / Inside the method

Each model is tested only on facts it already knows

EchoQA first asks each model the underlying fact directly and keeps only facts it answers correctly; the context then supplies a different, necessary fact. A later failure therefore cannot come from a missing prerequisite. Questions are multiple choice with an explicit Unknown option, so the unknown-answer rate (U_R) measures abstention on questions the model has the knowledge to answer.

The answer key is Noctuidae; the printed response also uses an Unknown option. Abstention rates for all six models and four conditions are in the results table under Evidence.

Instructions are progressively enforced. The Neutral Instruction (NI) already asks the model to combine the information with its own knowledge; Trust Yourself (TYI) adds that the information is insufficient, or that the model should prefer its own knowledge under conflict; Speak Out Loud (SOLI) makes it state that knowledge first. A golden-knowledge condition puts every needed fact in the context.

Each relationship demands different behavior: keep a known fact against fabricated context, combine both sources when they complement each other, and ignore irrelevant context. No fixed preference for memory or context satisfies all three.

  1. 01

    Establish known facts

    First test each model without context and retain knowledge it can answer, creating a model-specific starting point.

  2. 02

    Control the relationship

    Construct supportive, complementary, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts across scientific, factual, and commonsense knowledge.

  3. 03

    Measure information use

    Compare answer accuracy and uncertainty under different instructions, including prompts encouraging the model to use its own knowledge.

03 / Reading the evidence

Complementary context raises abstention on known facts

  • 62.72%

    Answers marked unknown

    Llama 3.1-70B's unknown-answer rate rises from 23.89% without context to 62.72% with complementary scientific context under neutral instructions.

  • 23.88%

    After instruction changes

    Encouraging the same model to trust its own knowledge lowers that uncertainty, although improved prompting does not eliminate the integration problem.

The pattern is not specific to one model. With complementary scientific context and the neutral instruction, the unknown-answer rate rises above its no-context level for every tested model except OpenAI o1, and at least doubles for the Llama and Qwen models. Writing all required facts into the context lowers it for every model, so the difficulty lies in drawing on memory once context is present.

In 200 random Llama 3.1-70B failures, questions it answered alone but missed with complementary context, the model relied only on the context and answer choices in 93.5% of cases. The authors hypothesize that instruction tuning, which trains answers from either context or memory, contributes to this behavior.

Unknown-answer rate U_R (%) for complementary reasoning on ALCUNA (scientific knowledge): the share of answers marked Unknown on questions whose prerequisite fact the model answered without context. w/o K = no context; NI = Neutral Instruction with the complementary context; TYI = Trust Yourself Instruction; Gold K = all required knowledge, including the elicited parametric fact, written into the context. Research summary

Large language models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of knowledge during pre-training (parametric knowledge, or PK) and can further be enhanced by incorporating contextual knowledge (CK). Can LLMs effectively integrate their internal PK with external CK to solve complex problems? In this paper, we investigate the dynamic interaction between PK and CK, categorizing their relationships into four types: Supportive, Complementary, Conflicting, and Irrelevant. To support this investigation, we introduce EchoQA, a benchmark spanning scientific, factual, and commonsense knowledge. Our results show that LLMs tend to suppress their PK when contextual information is available, even when it is complementary or irrelevant. While tailored instructions can encourage LLMs to rely more on their PK, they still struggle to fully leverage it. These findings reveal a key vulnerability in LLMs, raising concerns about their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks.
